recall.def: Retrieving information with few cues, as on a fill-in-the-blank or essay question.

recognition.def: Identifying information you have seen before among options, as on a multiple-choice question. It is usually easier than recall.

retrieval-cue.def: Any stimulus, such as a word, smell, place or photo, that helps bring a stored memory back.

context-dependent.def: Better recall when the external setting at retrieval matches the setting where the memory was formed.

state-dependent.def: Better recall when your internal state (calm, sleepy, after caffeine or a drug) at retrieval matches your state when you learned.

mood-congruent.def: The tendency to recall memories that match your current mood, such as sad memories when you feel sad.

retrieval-practice.def: Studying by pulling information out of memory, such as self-quizzing or writing what you remember, instead of rereading it.

testing-effect.def: The finding that retrieving information, as on a practice test, strengthens long-term memory more than spending the same time restudying it.

metacognition.def: Thinking about your own thinking, including judging how well you know something and choosing how to study.
